anchors.exact: How Positionality Influences Satire
When the Joke Is on You

nodes.label: The title asserts that a humorist's positionality influences what satire does.
nodes.note: The title claim is carried entirely by the article's central thesis (C2) and its recommendations (C16).
nodes.where: Title (b2–b3)

anchors.exact: this article will argue that these effects depend upon the would-be humorists’ positionality
This article argues that when such humor is used by marginalized individuals to critique power structures, it provides the epistemic friction necessary to expand knowledge and address injustice.
This indicates the subtle mechanisms by which positionality determines whether satire and irony become either effective social critique or a form of disparagement humor.

nodes.label: Baldwin argues that the sociopolitical function of ironic or satirical humor depends on the humorist's positionality: from marginalized critics of power it generates epistemic friction and subverts, while from privileged users against marginalized groups or social-justice work it generates no friction and preserves privilege.
nodes.note: This is a conceptual/philosophical argument. Its support is a synthesis of cited theory (Dotson, Medina, Bailey, humor scholarship), selected literary and media examples, and two academic-hoax case studies; no empirical test of audience effects is offered.
nodes.where: Abstract (b6); Social Power of Humor (b19); Television and Social Media (b79)

anchors.exact: humor, in particular irony and satire, when used in the service of criticizing oppressive power structures and especially by members of marginalized groups, is a potentially powerful tool for increasing receptivity and recognition of other ways of knowing and experiencing society
ironic, satirical, and double-voiced humor is powerful in its ability to defamiliarize established power structures and disrupt and destabilize hegemonic certainties
That humor can provide access to awareness that people do not already have makes it an extremely valuable social tool

nodes.flag: The claim is about effects on audiences (increasing receptivity, undermining active ignorance), but the support consists of theorists' accounts and readings of satirical texts; no observation of any audience becoming more receptive is offered, and the source does not rule out that the same satire is read literally or dismissed by the privileged listeners it hopes to reach (a risk Baldwin himself notes for irony in C7).
nodes.label: Baldwin claims that irony and satire used to criticize oppressive power structures, especially by marginalized people, are a potentially powerful tool for increasing receptivity to other ways of knowing, undermining active ignorance and effecting third-order epistemic change.
nodes.where: Epistemic Oppression and Humor (b13); Positionality and Humor (b38); Humor as It Effects Social Critique (b65)

anchors.exact: when these same ironic, satirical, double-voiced tools of humor are used by members of dominant groups to disparage, mock, or discredit marginalized groups or social-justice scholarship that seeks to make oppression visible, they serve no such purpose but rather perpetuate dominant epistemologies and power structures
abuses of this mode of humor by members of privileged groups who attack social-justice scholarship and activism are best understood as forms of superiority/disparagement humor

this style of mocking humor, levied from the privileged perch of the epistemically dominant, cannot be considered in the same light as the ironic, double-voiced satire that members of marginalized groups use to critique oppressive power structures

nodes.flag: The classification is made by the humorist's position and target rather than by any examined feature of the humor itself, so a privileged satirist who did engage substantively with social-justice claims would still be classed as producing disparagement; the source does not consider such a case. The supporting premise that social-justice scholarship 'arguably cannot' be a dominant epistemology (b83) is asserted rather than argued, and it matters because the whole distinction between subversion and disparagement turns on which side holds dominance.
nodes.label: Baldwin claims that when members of dominant groups use irony or satire to disparage marginalized groups or social-justice scholarship, it is not critique but superiority/disparagement humor that perpetuates dominant epistemologies and power structures.

nodes.note: The generalization is drawn from literary and cultural criticism of American women's humor, African-American humor and feminist art; it is offered as a tendency ('tends to characterize'), not a rule.
nodes.short: Irony marks marginalized humor; disparagement dominant

anchors.exact: postmodern irony (or that double-voiced, palimpsest mode of subversion) is vulnerable to being read literally and upholding the very structures of power it wishes to disrupt, complicate, or expand to include other voices
This is much less of a risk with satire.

nodes.label: Baldwin, following Shugart and Walker, holds that postmodern irony is politically ambiguous and vulnerable to being read literally so that it upholds the structures it means to disrupt, whereas satire, as 'militant irony' with an object of attack, carries much less of this risk.
nodes.note: This is the source's own caveat on the subversive power of irony. The assertion that satire is 'much less' at risk rests on Frye's definition (M3) rather than on any comparison of how ironic and satirical texts are actually received.
nodes.short: Irony can misfire; satire less so

anchors.exact: positionality, where it comes to utilizing humor for social critique, is to be understood not only in terms of the position individuals’ identity gives them within society but also the position they take in relation to social justice
both the humorists’ position on social justice and social position bear relevance

the positionality of the satirist becomes integral, both in terms of the position bestowed upon the individual by his or her identity and the status it is given in society and in terms of the position the individual takes in relation to other groups within society, oppressive power structures, and scholarship and activism for social justice

nodes.label: Baldwin claims that positionality is two-factored: it includes both the position an individual's identity confers in society and the stance the individual takes in relation to social justice.
nodes.note: The second factor is introduced to accommodate privileged satirists (Colbert, Stewart, Moore) who critique dominant narratives and marginalized people who uphold oppressive structures. A learner should notice that adding 'stance' means the function of a piece of satire can be determined by what it targets, which is what the thesis (C2) then predicts.

anchors.exact: The epitome of the shadow text is the academic hoax perpetrated against fields of scholarship that seek to disrupt power structures, challenge dominant epistemologies, and make oppression visible to those who are actively ignorant of it.

when an academic hoax takes the form of bad-faith pseudo-engagement, mimicry, and mockery of marginalized groups and scholarship that seek to make their oppression visible, committed by relatively privileged actors seeking to defend dominant epistemologies, it is much more akin to superiority/disparagement humor than to subversive satire

nodes.flag: The general account of hoaxes rests on Fredal's and Fleming and O'Carroll's characterizations plus two cases, both selected because they targeted social-justice scholarship (b93). No hoax aimed at a dominant field is examined, so the reader cannot tell whether the verdict follows from the hoax form or from the target; the source also concedes in passing (b95, b98) that Sokal's critiques had validity without saying how that bears on the shadow-text verdict.
nodes.label: Baldwin claims that the academic hoax against social-justice-oriented scholarship is the most literal shadow text: feigned engagement offering no epistemic friction, which when committed by privileged actors is closer to disparagement humor than to subversive satire and is a breach of academic ethics.
nodes.short: Academic hoax is ultimate shadow text

anchors.exact: the rationale given by Sokal himself, which depends upon his positionality as a physicist (dominant scientific epistemology) criticizing potentially disrupting postmodern social commentary (alternative marginalized epistemology)

anchors.exact: I make recommendations for those engaged in social-justice pedagogy to take humor seriously regarding its dual functions and impacts within the classroom, in popular culture, and even within the academic canon
At a minimum, such work should engage with its targets’ foundational claims on their own terms.

the positionality of humorists, hoaxers, and satirists—both in terms of identity and stance regarding justice-oriented initiatives—must be considered in the evaluation of any work produced in this vein

Individual professors and university administrators can introduce simple but formalized methods for adjudicating and then sanctioning members of culturally dominant groups who misuse irony, satire, hoaxes, and double-voiced humor to preserve hegemony over their own epistemic terrain and inhibit the ability of marginalized groups to contribute to knowledge production.

nodes.flag: The move from diagnosing shadow texts to institutional adjudication and sanctions is not argued for: no criteria for distinguishing 'misuse' from disagreement are offered beyond Applebaum's engagement/denial distinction, no consideration of error costs or of who adjudicates is given, and the source mentions that FIRE challenged Weber's classroom guidelines (b108) without addressing the objection. What would close the gap is a stated standard of adjudication and some evidence that such sanctions reduce the harms Bailey describes.
nodes.label: Baldwin recommends that those engaged in social-justice pedagogy take humor's dual functions seriously; that any work addressing social-justice scholarship engage its foundational claims on their own terms; that the positionality of humorists, hoaxers and satirists be considered in evaluating their work; and that professors and administrators adopt formal methods to adjudicate and sanction members of dominant groups who misuse humor to preserve hegemony.
nodes.short: Engage on own terms; consider positionality; sanction misuse

nodes.label: Baldwin acknowledges a difficulty: shadow texts must be identified and demonstrated, yet doing so risks encouraging them or recentering the needs of privileged groups, and extending the expectation of earnest engagement beyond academia will be less straightforward.

anchors.exact: Epistemic oppression, Kristie Dotson tells us, “refers to a persistent and unwarranted infringement on the ability to utilize persuasively shared epistemic resources that hinder one’s contributions to knowledge production”
privileged individuals become unable to spot bias or error and develop three vices—epistemic arrogance, epistemic laziness, and closed-mindedness—that Medina summarizes with the term active ignorance
Beneficial epistemic friction, to Medina, forces an individual “to be self-critical, to compare and contrast one’s beliefs, to meet justificatory demands, [and] to recognize cognitive gaps” (51).

nodes.label: Baldwin's analytic framework takes Dotson's definition of epistemic oppression and Medina's concepts of active ignorance (arrogance, laziness, closed-mindedness) and beneficial epistemic friction as the criteria by which humor is judged subversive or oppressive.
nodes.note: Whether a piece of humor 'generates epistemic friction' is never operationalized or measured; it is inferred from the humorist's position and target.
nodes.short: Dotson/Medina framework: friction and active ignorance
nodes.where: Epistemic Oppression and Humor (b8, b12); Television and Social Media (b78)

anchors.exact: [It] is a form of worldview protection: a willful resistance to knowing that occurs predictably in discussions that threaten a social group’s epistemic home terrain
Bailey defines shadow texts in classroom contexts as a form of “discursive resistance” that offers no epistemic friction but only serves as an obstacle (Bailey 2017).

nodes.label: Baldwin adopts Bailey's definitions of privilege-preserving epistemic pushback (willful resistance to knowing in discussions that threaten a group's epistemic home terrain) and shadow texts (discursive resistance that walks alongside social-justice concepts without engaging them) as the categories into which privileged satire is sorted.
nodes.note: Bailey's concept was developed for classroom contexts; Baldwin extends it to television, social media and academic hoaxes.

unlocated.exact: “The word ‘shadow’ calls to mind the image of something walking closely alongside another thing without engaging it”

nodes.where: Humor as Privilege-Preserving Epistemic Pushback (b69); Television and Social Media (b78–b79)

anchors.exact: describes satire as “militant irony” (Frye 1957, 223)
he identified two essential qualities of satire: wit or humor and an object of attack (Frye 1944, 76)
the academic hoax fits Frye’s broad definition of satire

nodes.label: Baldwin uses Frye's definition of satire—'militant irony' with two essential qualities, wit or humor and an object of attack, founded on the grotesque or absurd—to classify both subversive satire and the academic hoax as satire.
